title: Printing the News in 1776
description: Explore the printed documents, tools, and public announcements associated with American independence.
cardDescription: Explore the printed documents, tools, and public announcements associated with American independence.
focus: This scene centers on printing and the Declaration of Independence. The clues distinguish a document, the people preparing it, and the tools used to make copies.
solvingTip: Look for familiar paper-and-ink words first. A clue naming a historical person or document gives a more specific answer.
words: Document announcing the colonies' independence in 1776
Thomas who drafted much of the Declaration of Independence
Benjamin known as a printer and a member of the Declaration's drafting committee
Single large printed sheet intended for public display
Raised letters arranged for printing a page
Machine used to transfer an inked impression onto paper
Colored fluid spread onto printing letters
Sheet material receiving a printed impression
Person who sets and produces printed material
Short separately published work with a small number of pages
Assembly that adopted the Declaration of Independence
Territory governed by another country before independence
A person's handwritten name on a document
Preliminary version of a document before revision

answerNotes.DECLARATION: The Declaration announced a break with Britain. It did not by itself establish equal legal rights for everyone living in the new nation.
answerNotes.JEFFERSON: Thomas Jefferson was the principal drafter, working within a committee and a Congress that debated and revised the text.
answerNotes.FRANKLIN: Benjamin Franklin worked as a printer and served on the committee that prepared the Declaration. These clues connect a trade with a public role.
answerNotes.BROADSIDE: A broadside is printed on a large sheet for display or distribution. It is a format, not the name of one particular document.
answerNotes.TYPE: Movable type consists of separate printing characters. Here type names physical pieces rather than a category of object.

title: Joining the Rails at Promontory
description: Visit the railroad scene where the first US transcontinental rail connection was completed in 1869.
cardDescription: Visit the railroad scene where the first US transcontinental rail connection was completed in 1869.
focus: The clues combine the meeting at Promontory Summit in Utah with the parts and tools of a nineteenth-century railroad. They describe a historical connection, not a current timetable.
solvingTip: Start with physical railway objects. Some longer words identify equipment or the people doing particular jobs.
words: Large rail-fastening pin symbolically driven at the 1869 rail meeting
One of the long steel running surfaces beneath train wheels
Crosswise support beneath railroad running surfaces
Rail vehicle supplying the power to pull a train
Vapor that powered many nineteenth-century railway engines
Complete railway way formed by running surfaces and supports
Striking tool used to drive a track fastening
Railway station building in traditional American usage
Group of workers assigned to a railroad job
Railroad worker who operates a locomotive in US usage
Traditional crew car formerly found at the rear of many freight trains
Goods transported by a railway rather than passengers
Railway indication telling a train whether or how to proceed

answerNotes.UTAH: The 1869 meeting took place in Utah Territory. The location is now in the state of Utah; statehood came later.
answerNotes.SPIKE: The ceremonial golden spike marked the meeting of the railroads. Ordinary track used practical fastenings rather than gold spikes throughout.
answerNotes.RAIL: Rails provide the running surfaces. Cross ties support and hold them in position.
answerNotes.TIE: In American railway usage, a tie is a crosswise support. It is called a sleeper in some other varieties of English.
answerNotes.LOCOMOTIVE: A locomotive supplies the pulling power. In the nineteenth-century scene, steam locomotives were prominent, but not every locomotive uses steam.

title: Letters and Telegraph Messages
description: Compare two historic ways of sending news: a posted letter and an electrical message carried along wires.
cardDescription: Compare two historic ways of sending news: a posted letter and an electrical message carried along wires.
focus: Mail clues name physical objects that travel. Telegraph clues name signals and equipment that transmit a message, so the two systems need different kinds of handling.
solvingTip: Decide whether the clue belongs to a paper letter or an electrical message. Shared communication words can help connect the two.
words: System sending coded electrical messages along wires
Surname associated with a dot-and-dash signaling code
Dated postal marking showing where or when an item was processed
Adhesive postage label attached to a mailed letter
Folded paper covering that holds a posted letter
Metal conductor carrying an electrical telegraph signal
System representing letters with agreed signal patterns
Short signal in a familiar telegraph alphabet
Long signal paired with a short one in Morse signaling
Hand-operated switch used by a telegraph sender
Written message enclosed and sent through the post
Delivery directions written on the outside of mail
Charge for carrying an item through the mail
Person who sends or receives messages at a telegraph station

answerNotes.TELEGRAPH: A wired telegraph sends signals rather than transporting the original sheet of paper. Operators could transcribe the received message.
answerNotes.MORSE: Morse code represents characters with short and long signals. Its name recalls Samuel Morse; the system also developed through others' contributions.
answerNotes.POSTMARK: A postmark records postal processing information. It is different from the stamp that indicates payment of postage.
answerNotes.STAMP: A postage stamp indicates payment toward mail service. A postmark is a processing mark rather than the same physical label.
answerNotes.ENVELOPE: An envelope encloses the letter and provides a place for the delivery address. The message inside and its outer covering are separate objects.

title: The Wright Brothers Take Flight
description: Explore the brothers, equipment, and coastal setting of the Wrights’ powered flights in 1903.
cardDescription: Explore the brothers, equipment, and coastal setting of the Wrights’ powered flights in 1903.
focus: The clues concern the Wright brothers and early aircraft. The 1903 flights were near Kitty Hawk, at Kill Devil Hills, rather than in the brothers’ Ohio hometown.
solvingTip: Use the brothers’ names and familiar aircraft parts as entry points. A word describing a trial or a machine part may be easier than a place name.
words: Surname of brothers Orville and Wilbur
Wright brother who piloted the 1903 Flyer first
Orville's brother and fellow aviation experimenter
North Carolina town near the Wrights' 1903 flight site, with spaces omitted
Aircraft flown without an engine during early flight experiments
Aircraft surface designed to produce lift
Rotating blades providing thrust on an early powered airplane
Person controlling an aircraft in flight
Aircraft having two main wings arranged one above the other
Tail part controlling an airplane's side-to-side nose movement
Power-producing machine on a powered aircraft
Name commonly used for the Wrights' 1903 aircraft
Trial made to observe how an aircraft design performs
Ohio city where the Wright brothers lived and worked

answerNotes.WRIGHT: Orville and Wilbur Wright worked together on controlled flight. The shared surname should not be confused with the ordinary word meaning correct.
answerNotes.ORVILLE: Orville piloted the first flight that day. The brothers took turns over four powered flights on December 17.
answerNotes.WILBUR: Wilbur worked with Orville on the aircraft and flight experiments. Both brothers flew on the day of their 1903 powered flights.
answerNotes.KITTYHAWK: The Wrights' famous flights were at nearby Kill Devil Hills. Kitty Hawk is the better-known neighboring town name, not the exact takeoff location.
answerNotes.GLIDER: The Wrights tested gliders before their powered Flyer. A glider can fly without its own engine, using aerodynamic lift.

title: Working Along the Erie Canal
description: Travel a historic water route through locks, towpaths, gates, and the boats that moved goods across New York.
cardDescription: Travel a historic water route through locks, towpaths, gates, and the boats that moved goods across New York.
focus: This scene concerns the Erie Canal and the vocabulary of canal transport. Locks change a boat’s water level; a towpath runs beside the waterway.
solvingTip: Separate the water-control structure from the route beside it. The geographic clues specify the New York canal setting.
words: Great Lake sharing its name with a New York canal
River connected with the eastern end of the Erie Canal route
Canal chamber that raises or lowers boats between water levels
Path beside a canal used by animals pulling boats
Broad flat-bottomed boat used to carry canal cargo
Movable barrier at the end of a navigation chamber
Draft animal historically used to pull some canal boats
Load of goods carried aboard a canal boat
New York city near the historic canal's eastern end
New York city at the western end of the original Erie Canal
Rope connecting a pulling animal or vessel to a boat
Widened sheltered water area for canal boats
Small watercraft that can travel through a canal

answerNotes.ERIE: Lake Erie is one of the Great Lakes. The canal's name refers to that lake, not to a type of boat.
answerNotes.HUDSON: The Hudson provided the route toward New York City. The historic canal connected the Buffalo and Albany areas rather than running directly to the ocean.
answerNotes.LOCK: A lock changes the level of water around a boat. Gates at its ends allow the boat to enter and leave the chamber.
answerNotes.TOWPATH: A towpath runs beside the water. In early canal transport, draft animals could pull a boat using a line.
answerNotes.BARGE: A barge carries goods on inland water. Its flat bottom and cargo role distinguish it from a pleasure sailboat.
